en: Until you reached the age of seven,
She had the young women taste your food
And carefully prepare each meal,
Making every limb of yours whole,
Leading you with her until you became a man.
Across countless roads of no return,
She had the routes reconnoitered,
And horses brought from afar.
She had you thrust spears at the enemy,
Drag your spear through their ranks,
And learn the enemy’s ways.
She made your spirit mighty
And made you sultan and khan of the Argyn.
While your mighty uncle lived,
You became a man of weighty renown;
You kept a royal court and became khan.
You became a worthy hero,
Sound in all your twelve limbs.
While you had such an uncle,
When did you ever lack anything?
Ruling the people and maintaining the realm,
You became a seasoned lion.
As for the remaining Kanchoro,
You anointed yourself with bloody fat,
To remove the wretch
From this world forever.
“Do not let him stir up strife through the ages;
Finish him and be done with it.
Champion of the holy old man,
My comrade, lion Bakai,
Make the child disappear,
And turn him into black earth.
Jamgyrchy of the Eshetek,
Kutunu, the very eldest,
And round-eyed Sarkangan,”—
When the stars shone bright,
At the hour when the people slept,
They took these men as envoys
And called upon the people to mediate.
“This child is my darling,” they said,
And pulled him from my hands.
When God was about to punish
My crazed, unruly mother’s intent,
The wretch’s purpose went astray.
Fearing she would harm the child,
They saved him from brutal torment
And pulled him from my hands.
They did not rightly heed my words,
But regarded me as an enemy
And had him taken from my hands.
They had him securely confined in a palace
Where not even a crow could fly,
Whose walls were guarded by lions,
And which even spirits could not cross.
From a city of Hindustan,
The mother of seventy sons,
The sovereign among women,
The noble matron Adalsur—
They summoned Adalsur.
They hung an amulet around his neck,
And entrusted him to Adalsur,
The holy old man’s Adalsur.
She set his crooked affairs right
And raised him with tender indulgence.
My whole body turned to blood,
And both my arms were palsied.
This wretched one, unable to drink kumiss,
Longed even for muddy water.
A sorrowful day arose and became my fate;
My mouth, which could not hold a grain of wheat,
Swelled to the size of a bull’s head.
My mouth, which could not hold a grain of millet,
Swelled to the size of a heifer’s head.
My strength waned as the days passed,
And I endured a dog’s humiliation.
I wished to die, but could not;
I sobbed, unable to give up my soul.
Suffering was heaped upon suffering,
And yesterday the tears from both my eyes
Streamed down over my breast.
The wide world became narrow;
This once-magnificent soul
Longed even for muddy water.
My valiant son was lost,
And Külchoro departed in grief,
His two hands bound,
His neck pierced through,
His back slashed by the foe.
My Chürök wept and beat herself;
Her fair breasts, round as apples,
Were split open by the lash.
They rode wretched mares, jolting along,
And hung loosely in their felt cloaks
When they were carried off as booty.
Our villages stood side by side;
Our birth cords were cut and our swaddling washed together—
From our roots onward, we were inseparable.
When we rode against the foe, our cries were one;
When we went to battle, our banner was one;
When we fought, our dust was one;
Our souls were close, our lives were one.
I told you to heed my words;
I told you to cast your eyes upon us.
The treasure left as a legacy,
Your bloodthirsty uncle and lion,
You joined with Er Kyyaz to destroy.
You burned and cast aside Keng-Kol,
And set a grievous fire among your kin.
You took Chachykey as booty,
And took the mourning widow for a wife.
You broke open the treasury and took the money;
You divided the Kyrgyz and took slaves.
You seized the mountain passes, spreading terror,
And laid waste to the people.
My son, you stained your spear with blood;
You destroyed your own uncle
And fastened this deed securely.
You burned my plane tree and raised an uproar;
You bound my sapling in black.
You exhausted my treasury and possessions
And brought all my laughter to an end.
Well indeed you honored your lord,
You bastard, by withering
The mother who gave you her breast!
I was tormented and beaten;
I pleaded with the wretch,
Parting my snow-white hair,
Letting milk flow from my white breast,
Showing the suffering I had endured,
And shedding tears from my eyes.
I exposed my scorched brow in humiliation,
My dress torn into countless strips,
My honored head brought low.
“You once stood as my eldest son;
Show me a little mercy,” I said.
Raising my sinking heart,
“Here is your nourishment, my son,” I said,
And showed him my breast.
I screamed, wept, and beat myself:
“Look upon this helpless old woman;
Take your wretched, humiliated mother
Under your sheltering shade.”
I went begging for mercy,
While black blood ran from my calves.
You put an end to your mother’s good fortune;
Inflicting endless torment and hell,
My son, you broke my hands and feet.
You made your mother a wretched slave
And turned all I saw into a misty night.
You sucked my blood like a leech;
You scattered and shattered, my son,
Countless treasures and boundless wealth,
And let the enemy seize my herds.
You twisted what had been straight,
And turned it into the chill of somber autumn.
You leveled my hilltop into a hollow
And scattered my livestock in feasting.
You became an enemy and turned away;
Leading so many of your own blood,
You spared none but burned them.
You kindled strange spectacles among my people;
Without once looking back, for the sake of one khan,
You made red blood flow like water.
You heaped up hell like a mountain
And slaughtered my whole company.
My witless son, sink into the earth!
You destroyed my blue-green fruit,
And cut down my tall banner;
Could any enemy do worse than you?
You broke my terraced garden,
And devastated my flourishing strength.
You raised a mighty calamity
And showed your own kin a stronger arm
Than ever you showed the enemy.
You felled the plane tree,
And brought down the towering mountain.
You left sixty young women and widows
Wailing without exception.
You displayed your senseless valor
And dressed the whole people in black.
Can a human being be like you?
You black-hearted madman—
Can such a one be called human?
Before the camel crossed the cliff,
My son, you gathered the Argyn to plunder.
You had your white-haired mother
Beaten by the Argyn.
You made my blood flow freely
And set my soul aflame.
When your mother had grown old,
You accustomed her to endless torment.
My mad son, sprung from my own eyes,
Was I to blame for some ancient blood-feud,
That you had me dragged by a blue-gray calf?
You roused my long-buried fury;
Old Bakai, venerable as your forefather,
Without killing or disposing of him,
You had dragged about like a wolf-game carcass.
When your mother wailed aloud,
You had her breast split open.
You inflicted utter humiliation;
An enemy would be far better than you.
You made the torment surpass all bounds,
And made sorrow flourish in my heart.
You had me dragged by a blue calf
And branded my breast.
You did it not once but a thousand times,
And made such strife that you surpassed
Every other son born of humankind.
You drenched my poor head in blood
And sheared my hair like a mare’s.
In my old age you punished me
And reduced my food to scraps.
You left me no more than a spoonful of blood
And scorched my soul.
You ruined and scattered my herds;
You bent my waist fivefold.
Bringing calamity upon this head,
You deeply wounded my heart.
Though I begged, you did not heed my words;
You darkened all my days,
And stirred up, my foal, every last trace
Of my far-distant fury!
You created the most terrible strife,
Let it become a deed never forgotten.
Let his world collapse and be leveled;
Let his affairs burn and be set right.
For the many souls who will remain behind,
Let the destroyer of nations perish,
And let the people’s affairs prosper!”
Your beloved mother Kanykey,
Her wrath full against Kanchoro,
Spoke openly of the enemy,
Every word taking a different turn.
If you attend to every word,
Each word of your wise, fierce mother,
If you consider every word,
Was like a thrust of a spear.
Külchoro, son of Külüstan—
Against Külchoro himself
Her aspect was stern, her venom strong,
Able to humble anyone who opposed her;
So Kanykey stood urging them on.
Her grief and anguish broke open,
The turmoil within her burst forth,
Her eyes opened wide as bowls.
Without another word or sound,
Your dear mother fell silent,
And Kanykey abandoned her speech.
Then the noble-born Aichürök—
I, the wretched one, began to speak.
Taken as booty by the enemy,
Her heart scorched because of the foe,
The grief-stricken unfortunate woman
Cast forth her heavy sorrow.
